book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

chapters.file: ch05 - Introduction Contemplating a House of Cards.md
chapters.relation: The editor's introduction frames House of Cards as dramatizing the anxiety that politics cannot deliver justice: Frank's cold-blooded mercy killing of the injured dog in the pilot, his devouring of ribs at Freddy's like a lion among lamb-politicians, and his impunity-ridden rise ('Democracy is so overrated') all transgress our moral commitments. It argues the show taps real worries — inequality, corporate influence, the unfulfilled postracial promise — and that the book answers them with the contemplative life, withdrawing from action to think before returning. It closes on Plato and Aristotle's claim that philosophy begins in wonder, and that 'wonder begets courage.'

chapters.file: ch06 - PART I SOCRATES, PLATO, AND FRANK.md

chapters.relation: Ketchen and Yeo read the show's cynicism as Thrasymachus's challenge in Books 1-2 of the Republic — 'justice is the advantage of the stronger' — under which the just (Blythe, Lucas Goodwin) are dupes while the crafty win. Frank's proprietary 'my people' politics replays the shepherd-sheep exchange: Russo, Stamper, Sharp and the Gaffney constituents are a flock groomed, fleeced, and slaughtered (the naval base closure), just as Thrasymachus says shepherds fatten sheep for their masters. Frank's Sentinel ring makes him Glaucon's Ring of Gyges craftsman — perfectly unjust with a reputation for justice from the library dedication — while Lucas Goodwin is the just man made to seem unjust and destroyed. Yet against Petrov, Frank shows a conscience and tortured questions about justice in church, so the chapter ends with Republic Book 9: the tyrant, isolated and abandoned by Season 3's close, lives 'the worst sort of life.'

Gray argues Frank's fourth-wall asides dramatize Plato's being-versus-seeming distinction: the camera confidences reveal the true motive behind the public performance, as in the Blythe education-bill martyrdom gambit, the deliberately failed persuasion of Walker over the special prosecutor, and the seduction letter typed on the Underwood typewriter. The chapter reads Frank as winning the Ring of Gyges bet — enjoying adultery, corruption, and murder while seeming good — exactly the outcome the Republic sets out to refute. Against this it sets Socrates' examined life and Apology profession of ignorance: Frank pursues power without asking to what end, and his mastery of rhetoric over knowledge makes him the Sophist of the Gorgias rather than Plato's true politician, with Machiavelli's dissembling prince as his model.

chapters.file: ch09 - PART II IMAGINING POSSIBILITIES AMERICAN IDEALS IN HOUSE OF CARDS.md

chapters.relation: Kogelmann argues that political philosophers' ideal theory rests on Rawls's 'strict compliance' assumption — the West Wing picture where citizens and politicians pursue the public good — while House of Cards depicts the reality: Russo's zoning constituent, the teachers' union fighting performance standards, Senator Haas and Sharp's colleagues trading votes for self-interest. By the theory of the second best, ideals designed for selfless politicians misfire in a world with Frank and Remy Danton in it, so he recruits the older 'every man a knave' tradition — Adam Smith's self-love turned to public benefit, Hume's maxim, Madison's ambition-countering-ambition, Buchanan's 'politics without romance' — to redesign institutions against rent-seeking (SanCorp's purchase of votes on Russo's watershed bill) and politicians' short election-cycle horizons (Claire courting Senator Mendoza), via public financing and balanced-budget and inflation rules.

Palm and Stikkers read the Underwoods through James Truslow Adams's American dream as a question of values gone rotten: lacking ends, they pursue power for its own sake while repressed longings (Frank's Sentinel camaraderie, song, and friendship; Claire's motherhood — 'What will we leave behind?') erupt as the ressentiment Nietzsche introduced and Max Scheler systematized, hating those who embody the sacrificed values. Claire's hatred thus targets Gillian Cole's pregnancy and integrity (fired, then threatened with letting her child 'wither and die') and Adam Galloway's freedom and love — Scheler's pedestal-smashing pattern — after the slave-morality-like repression of her normal human affects. The ressentiment finally shatters when Michael Corrigan refuses to betray himself and hangs himself in Petrov's cell: Claire tells the cameras the truth and walks out on Frank at the end of Season 3, free of the resentment.

chapters.file: ch12 - PART III CHARACTERIZING FRANK ÜBERMENSCH OR THE PRINCE.md

chapters.relation: Aarons argues Frank is a Nietzschean Übermensch figure delivered through postmodern technique: the metafictional wave in 'Chapter 1,' self-referential mirror monologues ('Did you think I've forgotten you?'), and the flattening of affect in Zoe's death at the train station. Zarathustra's fearless overman, contrasted with the comfort-loving last man, maps onto Frank's 'hunt or be hunted' creed and his 'money is the McMansion in Sarasota... power is the old stone building' will-to-power, played out on Russo, Zoe, and Walker. The Genealogy's birds of prey and lambs frame Russo's Christian hypocrisy, and The Antichrist's equation of good with heightened power explains the church scene where Frank spits on the crucifix and leaves with the statue's ear — 'I've got God's ear now.'

Meyer mounts the counter-case: Frank exemplifies Nietzsche's master type (good as good-for-him, 'no longer are we bound by allegiances') and Russo the slave type ('he who cannot command himself is commanded'), but the overman is a synthesis of neither. He corrects the Leopold-and-Loeb 'above the law' reading and the Cesare Borgia identification: the genuine overman sublimates strong drives into creation — Goethe's self-discipline, Beethoven's new norms — and affirms other wills in themselves rather than as instruments, which Frank never does with Zoe, Peter, or Claire. Frank's revenge-driven scheming is slave-like psychological warfare, ruling others is the 'pettiest' form of power, and by Season 3 he is the slave of his own presidency — destructive without creating, and lacking even amor fati.

Littmann tests Frank against The Prince and largely confirms the 'Machiavellian' label: his lies (playing the loyal confidant while engineering Walker's fall), his strategic murders of Russo and Zoe, his preference for weaker allies, and his manufactured piety and father stories all enact Machiavelli's advice that a prince must learn 'not to be good' while seeming merciful, faithful, and religious. But the debts run both ways: Claire's vindictive 'let's make him suffer' offends Machiavelli's pamper-or-crush rule, and modern democratic image politics (Obama donating his Nobel money, the Obama-as-Muslim smear) outperforms The Prince where voters punish fear and reward a generosity Machiavelli thought ruinous. The moral is not despair but vigilance: since Underwoods will always rise, citizens must reward genuine results rather than respond to images.

Fallis walks through the education-reform arc — leaking Blythe's draft, gutting collective bargaining ('I revised the parameters of my promise'), framing Rasmussen in the speakership coup, the staged brick incident, and goading Spinella into felony assault — to show Frank follows Machiavelli's counsel to be 'other than good.' Yet Frank fails at Machiavelli's how and why: he never cultivates the appearance of integrity (Blythe, Feng, and Vasquez refuse to deal with a known liar), he inspires hatred as well as fear, and he seeks power for its own sake rather than the stability of the state, which makes the BBC's Francis Urquhart the superior Machiavellian. Even the revisionist readings of The Prince — Benner's irony, Rousseau's claim that Machiavelli was exposing princes' methods like an investigative reporter, Dietz's deliberate-sabotage thesis — would not rescue Frank, since he bungles the techniques regardless of their intent.

Perry frames Frank through Walzer's problem of dirty hands, taking its name from Sartre's play ('I have dirty hands right up to the elbows... Do you think you can govern innocently?') and Machiavelli's advice to 'enter into evil when forced by necessity' — the pilot's mercy killing of the dog and 'just shy of treason, which is politics' being the show's emblems. He maps the field onto the show: utilitarians for whom breaking rules can be right, absolutists like the bishop ('Love God, and love each other. Period.'), and Walzer's later 'supreme emergency' threshold deontology applied to Frank's child-killing drone strike and his desperate deal with Petrov in the Jordan Valley. The verdict: Frank's only edge over Heather Dunbar is a proven capacity to dirty his hands when needed, but he lacks the scruples that keep that capacity from becoming routine wrongdoing, so he is probably still the wrong man for the job.

chapters.file: ch18 - PART IV CLASSICAL LIBERALISM AND DEMOCRACY.md

chapters.relation: Courtland uses Hobbes's 'Foole' from Leviathan — who grants that covenants exist but insists injustice 'may sometimes stand with reason' — as the template for Frank, who enjoys the benefits of the social contract (security, cooperation, even Freddy's BBQ) while befriending and betraying Russo, Zoe, and Walker up to outright murder. Applying Hobbes's reply, the chapter audits both murders as contingency-ridden blunders — fingerprints, witnesses, cameras, forensic evidence, and the 'tells' of high-stakes deception — and diagnoses Frank's confidence as the vainglory behind Kavka's 'Foole's gold.' Even his success proves nothing: in the Latin Leviathan a fortunate outcome of reckless action is still imprudence, and his 'kingdom' rests on loose ends (Skorsky, Orsay, Tusk, Stamper, and Claire) that could bring the house of cards down.

Michels reads Frank as 'Hobbesian to the core' and democracy as 'the state of nature with elections': Walker, Matthews, and Vasquez show that elections elevate mediocrities, while Frank's America Works and his FEMA/Stafford Act end-run around Congress display the energetic sovereign for whom 'a tyrant is only a king disliked.' Hobbes's pleasure-pain psychology of appetite and aversion explains the cast — Frank's ribs, PlayStation, and pure taste for power; Russo's indiscriminate addictions; Doug's serial ones — while Hobbes's competition for gain, fear, and glory structures the Tusk money-versus-power war whose casualties include Freddy. With Hobbes's subordination of religion to civil power, Frank's crucifix-spitting 'I pray to myself, for myself' caps the case that truth only obstructs sovereignty, leaving Madison's 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition' as the lone check.

Shea argues the Underwoods' rise is structurally guaranteed rather than far-fetched, surveying democracy's critics: Plato's Republic Books 8-9 has the kallipolis of philosopher-guardians decay through timocracy and oligarchy into democracy, where a 'protector'-tyrant like Frank exploits the drones and the people's love of freedom (Russo as the prototypical democratic soul, Tusk as the oligarch-in-fact), while the tyrant ends fear-ridden and friendless — precisely Frank's Season 3. Hobbes and Hegel then reverse the verdict, arguing monarchy aligns the ruler's private interest with the public good and lets a people will as one instead of a formless mass — the insight Tom Yates has about voters identifying with the Underwoods as people — and Marx reframes it economically: SanCorp, Tusk, and Feng are the capitalist structure, and Frank's AmWorks, entitlement cuts, and nationalization threats show self-interested politicians siding with a growing proletariat. Against all four, Mill's Considerations on Representative Government supplies the democratic reply — responsiveness, better information, and citizen participation mean an Underwood cannot last if we keep fair elections, a free press, and real checks.

holes.name: Thrasymachus
holes.what: The Sophist in Book 1 of Plato's Republic who defines justice as 'the advantage of the stronger' and holds the unjust life preferable to the just.
holes.why: Chapter 7 reads Frank's cynical politics as Thrasymachus's challenge — his shepherd critique, his praise of injustice, and the tyrant as model politician structure the whole essay, not merely Plato's reply.

holes.name: Public Choice Theory (politics without romance)
holes.what: The program, running from Hume's maxim that every man 'ought to be supposed a knave' to James Buchanan, of modeling politicians and voters as self-interested when designing political institutions.
holes.why: Chapter 10's positive proposal — design the ideal society assuming people like Frank run for office, countering rent-seeking and politicians' short-termism — is public-choice reasoning against Rawlsian ideal theory.

holes.name: Max Scheler
holes.what: German phenomenologist who extended Nietzsche's account of ressentiment, locating its modern source in the industrial ethos of capitalism rather than Christianity.
holes.why: Chapter 11 analyzes Frank and especially Claire Underwood through Scheler's Ressentiment — the systematic repression of affects, value delusions, and the impulse to smash pedestals — more than through Nietzsche's own texts.

holes.name: The American Dream
holes.what: James Truslow Adams's ideal of a better and richer life open to everyone according to ability rather than birth, which Adams warned was decaying into mere materialism and means without ends.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues the show depicts the American dream perverted into power for its own sake, with Claire's ressentiment springing from the loftier values she sacrificed to it.

holes.name: Postmodernism (metafiction and self-referentiality)
holes.what: The aesthetic-philosophical movement rejecting Enlightenment faith in progress, playing with fiction and reality through irony and parody — here metafiction, self-referentiality, and flattening of affect.
holes.why: Chapter 13 reads Frank's fourth-wall asides, his wave to the viewer, and Zoe's graphic death as postmodern techniques that implicate the audience in his nihilism.

holes.name: The Problem of Dirty Hands
holes.what: The problem, named from Sartre's play and formulated by Michael Walzer, that politicians sometimes must do what is genuinely wrong, and must then acknowledge guilt and accept public punishment.
holes.why: Chapter 17 judges whether Frank or Heather Dunbar is fit to rule precisely through Walzer's dirty-hands test, supreme emergency, and threshold deontology.
